opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that for these two directions, the sequencing is different, and getting it wrong is one of the easiest ways to kill a company.

For world models, the research risk is still very high. We don't fully agree on what a world model even *is*: a video predictor, a latent dynamics model, something more structured that captures causality and physics? If you commercialize too early, you lock yourself into one interpretation, usually whatever demos well, like pretty video generation, and the business pressure pulls you away from the harder questions. So I'd lean research-first, but with a clear internal "north star" task, something like robot manipulation or scientific simulation, where you can tell whether the model really understands the world or is just interpolating pixels.

Auto research is a bit different. The pieces are already useful today, even if the full vision of an AI scientist is far off. Literature synthesis, experiment design, running and debugging code, analyzing results: each can save researchers real time now. So I think you can commercialize in parallel, as long as the product is a *wedge* into the research and not a detour. Every user running experiments gives you trajectories: what worked, what failed, how humans corrected the agent. That data is exactly what you need to improve the system. Commercialization becomes part of the research loop.

The general principle I'd suggest is to ask: does revenue generate the right signal? If customers push you toward the problems you'd want to solve anyway, commercialize early, because it's free alignment between business and science. If customers pull you toward short-term features that are orthogonal to the core question, protect the research longer and raise money on the vision instead.

There's also a cultural point. Researchers often think commercialization is a distraction, and business people think research is a black hole. In a company like this you need people who can live in both worlds, who can look at a customer complaint and say, "Ah, this is a symptom of a fundamental limitation in how the model represents the problem." That translation layer is where a lot of the real insight comes from.

So I'd summarize it this way: for world models, research-led with a grounded target; for auto research, product and research co-evolving, with the product designed as an instrument for learning. And in both cases, stay honest about which parts are solved and which aren't, because overpromising in this field burns trust very quickly.

r001.rationale: The response favors research-first for world models but gives no initial six-to-twelve-month research period.

r002.rationale: It discusses commercialization and cross-functional company culture, but does not propose a tangible prototype as the milestone for bringing in commercialization-experienced co-founders.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that for these two directions the sequencing is almost forced on you, and it's different for each.

For auto research, I'd say research has to come first, and it has to come first for a long time. The reason is that the thing you're selling isn't a feature, it's a capability that doesn't fully exist yet. Nobody will pay for an "AI scientist" that produces plausible-looking papers that are wrong. The entire value is in whether the discoveries hold up. So in the early phase, your product is actually your evidence. Can the system find something a human expert didn't know? Can it do it repeatedly, across domains, without someone babysitting it? Until you can answer yes with some confidence, commercialization is premature, and worse, it distorts the research. The moment you have paying customers, you start optimizing for what looks impressive in a demo instead of what's actually true, and in science that gap is fatal.

That said, I don't think "research first" means "no contact with the real world." The mistake I see is people treating these as sequential phases, like you do research for three years and then flip a switch. I'd rather have a thin layer of commercialization very early, but choose it deliberately. Pick a narrow domain where verification is cheap, where you can actually check if the model's output is correct, maybe materials, maybe certain parts of math, maybe some physics simulations. Use that as a forcing function. The customer isn't really there for revenue, they're there to keep you honest about what "working" means. The danger in pure research mode is that you define success yourself, and you'll always define it generously.

World models are a bit different. There the capability is more continuous. A world model that's seventy percent right is still useful for some things, for robotics, for simulation, for planning. So you can commercialize earlier, and the feedback loop is tighter. The risk there is the opposite one, that you commercialize too early into something narrow, say a video generation product, and then the revenue locks you into that path. You end up building a very good video model and never building a world model. The commercial pull and the research direction diverge, and the commercial one usually wins because it has a number attached to it.

So if I had to compress it: for auto research, research leads, commercialization follows but shows up early as a verification mechanism, not as a revenue strategy. For world models, they can run in parallel, but you have to be very disciplined about not letting the application define the model. In both cases the thing I'd watch is whether the commercial work is informing the research or replacing it. Informing is great. Replacing is how you end up with a company that's successful and completely uninteresting.

And honestly, I'd add one more thing. The people doing this need to be okay with being wrong in public for a while. Research means publishing things that get corrected. If the company culture can't tolerate that, you'll default to commercialization too early just because it feels safer. That's probably the biggest practical constraint, more than any technical one.

astra-6.text:
I think the sequencing depends on what the company still needs to prove. If the core research idea is uncertain, you need to give yourself room to test it. But I wouldn’t wait until the research feels complete to talk to users. Those conversations help you understand which capabilities would actually matter.

For Auto Research, I’d start with a narrow part of the research process where you can evaluate the output and where a researcher would find it useful today. That gives you a way to learn from real use while continuing toward more autonomous research. The danger is letting every customer request pull you into a different direction, so the initial product should also help answer your central research question.

For World Models, I’d apply the same principle: choose a setting where better predictions can lead to better decisions, and test that connection. A model can produce an impressive demonstration without being reliable enough to build a business around.

So I’d sequence it as a research hypothesis, a focused demonstration, and then a narrow product—with feedback between those stages. Commercialization should give you evidence and resources to advance the research. You want to avoid scaling the company before you’ve established that the technical capability creates value.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to sequence the uncertainties. With Auto Research or World Models, you have scientific uncertainty—can the system actually do what you hope?—and commercial uncertainty—does that capability solve a problem people will pay for? If you try to resolve both by building a big company immediately, you can spend a lot of money without learning very much.

I would start with a research milestone that makes the core idea testable. For Auto Research, can it complete a useful research loop and produce a result you can independently verify? For a world model, can it make predictions that improve decisions in a specific setting? A compelling demo is a starting point, but you want something repeatable.

At the same time, I would talk to potential users. You don’t need to wait until the research is finished to discover what matters to them. Once there’s a reliable capability, find a narrow application where it creates enough value that someone will pay for it. That application can give you feedback, data, and revenue to support the next stage of research.

So I wouldn’t say, finish all the research and then commercialize. I’d alternate: establish a capability, test its usefulness, and let what you learn inform the next research question. The important thing is to preserve room for the long-term research while making each commercial step useful on its own.
